title: Seeing Below the Limit of Light

scenes.tts: A good light microscope resolves a little over two hundred nanometres. Two neurons touching could not be told apart from one continuous network, because the gap between them is far below that. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light. So electron microscopy can ask what the fine structure of a cell is: its membranes, junctions, vesicles and organelles, at nanometre scale.
scenes.visual: Two touching cells with a yellow light-limit disc covering the gap; question of gap or network; long light wave beside a much shorter electron wave; the cell's fine structure appears as chips.

scenes.tts: First, fix the tissue. Glutaraldehyde mainly cross-links proteins. Osmium tetroxide reacts with membrane lipids, and it is heavy enough to add electron density. The fixative must diffuse in, so slow infiltration can distort membranes. Then solvent, acetone or ethanol, replaces the water. Last, resin soaks in and sets into a hard plastic block.
scenes.visual: A tissue piece moves through three beakers: fixative (arrows diffusing inward), solvent (water drops leave), resin (sets into a block).

scenes.tts: An ultramicrotome with a glass or diamond knife cuts sections roughly sixty to eighty nanometres thick. Serial sections lie in ribbons on a grid, so one cell can be followed from section to section. Sections are usually stained with uranyl acetate then lead citrate, which add contrast. The beam passes through the stained section and is absorbed and scattered. The image is a flat projection of a thin slice of dead, prepared tissue.
scenes.visual: Knife slices the block into thin sections that form a ribbon on a grid; one cell is followed across the ribbon; a section is stained; beam passes through, some stopped; the image forms below.

scenes.tts: Freezing is another route. High-pressure freezing stops cell activity quickly and suppresses damaging ice crystals. Scanning electron microscopy images surfaces instead of slices. In freeze-fracture, the specimen is frozen and fractured, and a platinum-carbon replica is made. The replica, not the tissue, goes in the microscope, and shows planar views of the internal organisation of membranes.
scenes.visual: Three panels: fast freezing, a beam scanning a surface, a fracture face with a replica lifted off.

scenes.tts: Here is a synapse, drawn as a schematic. Dark is where heavy metal bound. The two membranes stay separate across a cleft, so the synapse is a gap, not continuity. De Robertis and Bennett measured the cleft at ten to fifteen nanometres in 1955. Palay found about twenty nanometres in 1956. Small vesicles crowd the presynaptic side, and the postsynaptic membrane is thickened.
scenes.visual: A schematic micrograph panel (marked schematic): two dark membranes with a pale cleft, vesicles crowded on the presynaptic side, a thickened postsynaptic membrane; each feature labelled and the cleft measured.

scenes.tts: Fixation can create structures. In Bacillus cereus, conventional fixation gave pocket-like membrane invaginations that were absent after freezing and freeze substitution. The control is to confirm a structure with an independent preservation method. Every cell imaged is dead, and few cells are imaged in detail, so compare fixation methods and examine many cells.
scenes.visual: Two bacterial outlines: conventional fixation with pockets, freezing without; green control; then a few dead cells and the control of comparing methods and many cells.

scenes.tts: In 1954 Palade and Porter found the endoplasmic reticulum in situ in every cell type they examined. In 1955 Palade described dense particles, a hundred to a hundred and fifty angstroms, preferentially on its membranes in many cell types. In 1973 Heuser and Reese stimulated frog neuromuscular junctions at ten hertz and fixed samples. Membrane in vesicles fell thirty per cent at one minute and sixty per cent at fifteen minutes, and a tracer entered cisternae, then vesicles.
scenes.visual: Left: schematic reticulum sheets with dense particles on their membranes (Palade and Porter 1954; Palade 1955). Right: two bars, 30 and 60 percent loss, and a tracer entering a cisterna then vesicles (Heuser and Reese 1973).
scenes.caption: In 1954 Palade and Porter found the endoplasmic reticulum in situ in every cell type they examined. In 1955 Palade described dense particles, 100 to 150 Å, preferentially on its membranes in many cell types. In 1973 Heuser and Reese stimulated frog neuromuscular junctions at 10 Hz and fixed samples. Membrane in vesicles fell 30% at 1 minute and 60% at 15 minutes, and a tracer entered cisternae, then vesicles.

scenes.tts: In 1972 Kerr, Wyllie and Currie described apoptosis as distinct from necrosis: condensation and breakup into membrane-bound, well-preserved fragments. Keep this rule. Conventional electron microscopy shows structure in dead, fixed tissue, never motion. Confirm a structure with an independent preservation method.
scenes.visual: A cell condenses and breaks into membrane-bound fragments (Kerr, Wyllie and Currie 1972); then the rule appears in a box.
